questions.question: Consider a system of linear equations \(Ax = b\), where \[A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\sqrt{2} & 3 \\ -1 & \sqrt{2} & -3 \end{bmatrix}, \quad b = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}.\] This system of equations admits .
questions.explanation:
The augmented matrix \([A \mid B]\) for the given system of linear equations is: \[[A \mid B] = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\sqrt{2} & 3 & 1 \\ -1 & \sqrt{2} & -3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\] Applying the row operation \(R_2 \to R_2 + R_1\): \[= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\sqrt{2} & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\] \[\rho(A) = 1\] \[\rho(A \mid B) = 2\] Since \(\rho(A) \neq \rho(A \mid B)\), the system of equations is inconsistent. Therefore, there is no solution for \(x\). \[\boxed{\text{(C) no solutions for x}}\]
Key points
  • Rouché–Capelli Theorem: A system of linear equations \(Ax = b\) is consistent if and only if the rank of the coefficient matrix \(A\) is equal to the rank of the augmented matrix \([A \mid B]\).
  • If \(\rho(A) = \rho(A \mid B) = n\) (number of variables), the system has a unique solution.
  • If \(\rho(A) = \rho(A \mid B) < n\), the system has infinitely many solutions.
  • If \(\rho(A) < \rho(A \mid B)\), the system has no solution.

questions.question: Let \(\alpha, \beta\) be two non-zero real numbers and \(v_1, v_2\) be two non-zero real vectors of size \(3 \times 1\). Suppose that \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) satisfy \(v_1^T v_2 = 0\), \(v_1^T v_1 = 1\), and \(v_2^T v_2 = 1\). Let \(A\) be the \(3 \times 3\) matrix given by: \[A = \alpha v_1 v_1^T + \beta v_2 v_2^T\] The eigenvalues of \(A\) are .
questions.explanation: Given: \[A = \alpha V_1 V_1^T + \beta V_2 V_2^T\] Multiplying by \(V_1\) on both sides: \[AV_1 = \alpha V_1 V_1^T V_1 + \beta V_2 V_2^T V_1\] Since \(V_1^T V_1 = 1\) and \(V_2^T V_1 = 0\) (orthogonal vectors): \[AV_1 = \alpha V_1(1) + \beta V_2(0)\] \[AV_1 = \alpha V_1\] Comparing with the standard eigenvalue equation \(A\mathbf{x} = \lambda \mathbf{x}\), we find: One of the eigenvalue \(= \alpha\) Similarly, we can verify the other eigenvalues by multiplying by \(V_2\) and a third vector \(V_3\) orthogonal to both \(V_1\) and \(V_2\): \[AV_2 = \alpha V_1 V_1^T V_2 + \beta V_2 V_2^T V_2 = \alpha V_1(0) + \beta V_2(1) = \beta V_2\] \[AV_3 = \alpha V_1(0) + \beta V_2(0) = 0\] The eigenvalues are \(\alpha, \beta, 0\). \[\boxed{\text{(A) $0,\alpha, \beta$}}\]

questions.question: The function \(f(x) = 8 \log_e x - x^2 + 3\) attains its minimum over the interval \([1, e]\) at \(x = \_\_\_\_\_\_\). (Here \(\log_e x\) is the natural logarithm of \(x\).)
questions.explanation:
The given function is \(f(x) = 8 \log_{e} x - x^{2} + 3\) in the interval \([1, e]\). To find the extrema, we first find the derivatives: \[f'(x) = \dfrac{8}{x} - 2x\] \[f''(x) = -\dfrac{8}{x^{2}} - 2\] Setting \(f'(x) = 0\) to find critical points: \[\dfrac{8 - 2x^{2}}{x} = 0 \implies 8 - 2x^{2} = 0 \implies x^{2} = 4 \implies x = 2\] (Since the domain is \([1, e]\) and \(e \approx 2.718\), \(x = 2\) lies within the interval). Check the second derivative at \(x = 2\): \[f''(2) = -\dfrac{8}{4} - 2 = -4 < 0\] Since \(f''(2) < 0\), \(f(x)\) has a local maximum at \(x = 2\). To find the global minimum over the closed interval \([1, e]\), we evaluate the function at the boundaries: At \(x = 1\): \[f(1) = 8 \log_{e}(1) - (1)^{2} + 3 = 0 - 1 + 3 = 2\] At \(x = e\): \[f(e) = 8 \log_{e}(e) - (e)^{2} + 3 = 8(1) - e^{2} + 3 \approx 11 - 7.389 = 3.611\] Comparing the values \(f(1) = 2\) and \(f(e) \approx 3.611\), the minimum value occurs at \(x = 1\). \[\therefore \text{Global minimum at } x = 1\] \[\boxed{\text{(b)}\ \ 1}\]
Key points
  • Global Extrema on Closed Intervals: To find the absolute (global) maximum or minimum on \([a, b]\), compare the function values at all critical points in the interval and at the endpoints \(a\) and \(b\).
  • Local Maxima/Minima: A function has a local maximum at \(x = c\) if \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) < 0\). It has a local minimum if \(f'(c) = 0\) and \(f''(c) > 0\).

questions.question: The value of the integral \(\iint\limits_{D} 3(x^{2} + y^{2}) dx dy\), where \(D\) is the shaded triangular region shown in the diagram, is (rounded off to the nearest integer).
questions.explanation:
From the given region \(D\), the triangular area is bounded by the lines \(y = x\), \(y = -x\), and \(x = 4\). Due to the symmetry of the integrand \(3(x^2 + y^2)\) about the x-axis, we can evaluate the integral for the upper half and multiply by 2. \[\iint\limits_{D} 3(x^2 + y^2) dx dy = 2 \int_{x=0}^{4} \int_{y=0}^{x} 3(x^2 + y^2) dy dx\] \[= 6 \int_{0}^{4} \int_{0}^{x} (x^2 + y^2) dy dx\] \[= 6 \int_{0}^{4} \left\{ x^2 y + \dfrac{y^3}{3} \right\}_{y=0}^{x} dx\] \[= 6 \int_{0}^{4} \left\{ x^3 + \dfrac{x^3}{3} \right\} dx\] \[= 6 \int_{0}^{4} \dfrac{4x^3}{3} dx\] \[= 6 \left( \dfrac{x^4}{3} \right)_{0}^{4}\] \[= 2(4)^4\] \[= 512\] \[\boxed{512}\]
Key points
  • Double Integral Symmetry: If the region \(D\) and the integrand are symmetric about an axis, the integral can be simplified by calculating a portion and scaling.
  • Order of Integration: For a region bounded by \(x=k\) and \(y=f(x)\), setting the limits as \(\int_{x_{min}}^{x_{max}} \int_{y_{min}(x)}^{y_{max}(x)} dy dx\) is often the most direct approach.

questions.question: Consider the following partial differential equation (PDE) \[a \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2} + b \frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2} = f(x,y),\] where \(a\) and \(b\) are distinct positive real numbers. Select the combination(s) of values of the real parameters \(\xi\) and \(\eta\) such that \(f(x,y) = e^{(\xi x + \eta y)}\) is a solution of the given PDE.
questions.explanation: Given, \[f(x,y) = e^{(\xi x + \eta y)}\] Differentiating two times with respect to \(x\), \[\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2} = \xi^2 e^{(\xi x+\eta y)} = \xi^2 f(x,y)\] Differentiating two times with respect to \(y\), \[\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2} = \eta^2 e^{(\xi x+\eta y)} = \eta^2 f(x,y)\] Substituting into \[a\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial x^2} + b\frac{\partial^2 f(x,y)}{\partial y^2} = f(x,y)\] \[a\xi^2f(x,y) + b\eta^2f(x,y) = f(x,y)\] \[a\xi^2 + b\eta^2 = 1\] Checking option (A): \[\xi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}}, \qquad \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2b}}\] Then, \[a\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}}\right)^2 + b\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2b}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} = 1\] Hence, option (A) satisfies the equation. Checking option (B): \[\xi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a}},\qquad \eta = 0\] Then, \[a\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{a}}\right)^2 + b(0)^2 = 1\] Hence, option (B) also satisfies the equation. Similarly on checking, options (C) and (D) do not satisfy \(a\xi^2 + b\eta^2 = 1\) \[\boxed{\text{(A)}\ \xi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2a}} , \eta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2b}};\ \text{(B)}\ \xi = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{a}} , \eta = 0}\]

questions.question: A simple closed path \(C\) in the complex plane is shown in the figure. If \[\oint_{C} \frac{2^z}{z^2 - 1} \, dz = -i\pi A,\] where \(i = \sqrt{-1}\), then the value of \(A\) is (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: In the given question, \[f(z) = \frac{2^z}{z^2 - 1} = \frac{2^z}{(z-1)(z+1)}\] The singularity points where \(f(z)\) is not analytic lies at \(z = 1\) and \(z = -1\). Since, \(z = 1\) doesn't lie inside the contour \(C\). Hence, \[I = \oint_c \frac{2^z}{z^2 - 1} \, dz = \oint_c \frac{\left(\frac{2^z}{z-1}\right)}{z+1} \, dz\] \[I = 2\pi i \, [\text{Residue at } z = -1]\] \[I = 2\pi i \times \lim_{z \to (-1)} (z+1) \cdot \frac{2^z}{(z-1)(z+1)}\] \[I = 2\pi i \times \frac{2^{-1}}{(-1-1)} = -\frac{2\pi i}{4}\] \[\therefore I = -\frac{\pi i}{2}\] Given: \(I = -\pi i A\). Hence, \[A = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5\] \[\boxed{0.50}\]

questions.question: The current \(I\) in the circuit shown is .
questions.explanation:
Method Nodal Analysis
Let the voltage at node \(A\) be \(V_A\). Applying KCL at node \(A\), \[\frac{V_A}{2\,\text{k}\Omega} + \frac{V_A-5}{2\,\text{k}\Omega} = 10^{-3}\] \[2V_A-5 = 2\times10^3\times10^{-3}\] \[2V_A = 7 \ \Rightarrow \ V_A = 3.5~\text{V}\] The required current is \[I = \frac{5-V_A}{2\,\text{k}\Omega} = \frac{5-3.5}{2\times10^3} = 0.75\times10^{-3}~\text{A}\]
Method Superposition Theorem
Case 1: Only the \(5~\text{V}\) source is active
The current source is opened. \[I_1 = \frac{5}{2\,\text{k}\Omega+2\,\text{k}\Omega} = \frac{5}{4\times10^3} = 1.25\times10^{-3}~\text{A}\] Case 2: Only the \(10^{-3}~\text{A}\) current source is active
The voltage source is short-circuited. The \(10^{-3}~\text{A}\) current divides equally between the two identical \(2~\text{k}\Omega\) branches. \[I_2 = \frac{10^{-3}}{2} = 0.5\times10^{-3}~\text{A}\] The direction of \(I_2\) is opposite to the reference direction of \(I\). \[\Rightarrow I = I_1-I_2\] \[= 1.25\times10^{-3} - 0.5\times10^{-3} = 0.75\times10^{-3}~\text{A}\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }0.75\times10^{-3}~\text{A}}\]

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown in the figure with input \(V(t)\) in volts. The sinusoidal steady state current \(I(t)\) flowing through the circuit is shown graphically (where \(t\) is in seconds). The circuit element \(Z\) can be ~~~~~.
questions.explanation:
From the given waveform of the steady-state current \(I_{(t)}\), we can deduce the mathematical expression for the current. The peak amplitude of the current is: \[I_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{A}\] The waveform passes through zero going positive at a delayed time, reaching its peak at \(t = \frac{\pi}{4}\). Thus, the phase difference is \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) lagging. The time-domain expression for the current is: \[I_{(t)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sin\left(t - \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\,\text{A}\] Given that the input voltage is \(V(t) = \sin(t)\,\text{V}\), the current lags the voltage by \(\frac{\pi}{4}\). A lagging current signifies that the passive network contains inductive reactance. Hence, the load impedance can be represented as: \[Z = j\omega L\] The total circuit impedance seen by the source includes the series component, yielding: \[I(t) = \frac{V_{(t)}}{1 + Z} = \frac{\sin(t)}{Z + 1}\,\text{A} \quad \text{--- (i)}\] From the waveform, the maximum value of the current is: \[|I(t)|_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{A}\] Using the magnitude of the transfer function from equation (i): \[|I(t)|_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{|Z + 1|} = \frac{1}{|j\omega L + 1|} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\] Equating the denominators: \[|j\omega L + 1| = \sqrt{2}\] \[\sqrt{1 + \omega^2 L^2} = \sqrt{2}\] Squaring both sides: \[1 + \omega^2 L^2 = 2\] Here \(\omega = 1\,\text{rad/s}\): \[\therefore L^2 = 1\] \[\implies L = 1\,\text{H}\]
Key points
  • A sinusoidal current waveform of the form \(I_{m}\sin(\omega t - \phi)\) indicates a phase lag of \(\phi\) radians with respect to a standard reference sine wave \(\sin(\omega t)\).
  • In an AC circuit, an inductive load causes the steady-state current to lag behind the applied voltage.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse the peak value \(I_{\text{max}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\,\text{A}\) with the RMS value when calculating the magnitude equation.
  • Ensure that the phase delay from the time axis shifts properly into a negative phase angle in the sine argument.
\[\boxed{(b) \textit{an inductor of 1 H} }\]

questions.question: A linear 2-port network is shown in Fig. (a). An ideal DC voltage source of 10 V is connected across Port 1. A variable resistance R is connected across Port 2. As R is varied, the measured voltage and current at Port 2 is shown in Fig. (b) as a \(V_2\) versus \(-I_2\) plot. Note that for \(V_2= 5 V\), \(I_2= 0 mA\), and for \(V_2= 4 V\), \(I_2= -4 mA\) . When the variable resistance R at Port 2 is replaced by the load shown in Fig. (c), the current \(I_2\) is mA (rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
From figure (a) \(V_1 = 10\,\text{V}\). For this problem, we need to draw the Thevenin equivalent circuit as seen from Port 2. From plot in figure (b), the open-circuit voltage is: \[V_{oc} = 5\,\text{V} = V_{th}\] The slope of plot in figure (b) is calculated as: \[\text{Slope} = \frac{4 - 5}{4 - 0} \frac{\text{V}}{\text{mA}} = -0.25\,\text{k}\Omega = -250\,\Omega\] The equation of the \(V_2\) vs \(-I_2\) plot is: \[V_2 - 5 = -250(-I_2 - 0)\] \[V_2 = 5 + 250I_2\] When \(V_2 = 0\), the short-circuit current is derived from: \[I_2 = -\frac{5}{250} = -20\,\text{mA}\] Since \(I_{sc} = -I_2\): \[I_{sc} = 20\,\text{mA}\] The Thevenin impedance looking in from Port 2 is: \[Z_{th} = \frac{V_{oc}}{I_{sc}} = \frac{5\,\text{V}}{20\,\text{mA}} = 250\,\Omega\] We can now draw the resultant network with the load: The current \(I_2\) is calculated as: \[I_2 = \frac{10 - 5}{250 + 1000}\,\text{A} = \frac{5}{1250}\,\text{A}\] \[I_2 = 4\,\text{mA}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Unit Conversion: Pay close attention to the units on the graph axes (e.g., mA to A) to avoid a scale error in the impedance calculation.
  • Current Direction: Ensure the sign of \(I_2\) is correctly handled according to the port convention defined in the problem.
\[\boxed{3.9 \,\text{to}\, 4.1}\]

questions.subject: signals-and-systems
questions.question: The outputs of four systems (\(S_1, S_2, S_3, S_4\)) corresponding to the input signal \(\sin(t)\), for all time \(t\), are shown in the figure. Based on the given information, which of the four systems is/are definitely NOT LTI (linear and time-invariant)?
questions.explanation:
Given the system mappings: \[\sin(t) \xrightarrow{S_1} \sin(-t)\] \[\sin(t) \xrightarrow{S_2} \sin(t+1)\] \[\sin(t) \xrightarrow{S_3} \sin(2t)\] \[\sin(t) \xrightarrow{S_4} \sin^2(t)\] For an LTI system, the input & output frequency must be the same with amplitude & phase change. \(S_1\) & \(S_2\) can be LTI. For \(S_3\): \[x(t) = \sin t \rightarrow y(t) = \sin 2t\] I/P frequency = \(1\,\text{rad/sec}\) O/P frequency = \(2\,\text{rad/sec}\) \(\rightarrow\) Definitely not LTI For \(S_4\): \[x(t) = \sin t \rightarrow y(t) = \sin^2 t = \frac{1 - \cos 2t}{2}\] \(x(t)\) is input frequency = \(1\,\text{rad/sec}\) \(y(t)\) is output frequency \(\Rightarrow \omega = 0\) & \(2\,\text{rad/sec}\) \(\rightarrow\) Definitely not LTI \(S_3\) and \(S_4\) are definitely not LTI. \[\boxed{S_3 \text{ and } S_4}\]
Key points
  • An LTI system cannot generate new frequency components. It can only modify the amplitude and phase of the existing input frequencies.
  • If the input is \(x(t) = A\sin(\omega_0 t)\), the output of an LTI system must be of the form \(y(t) = B\sin(\omega_0 t + \phi)\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Assuming non-linear operations like squaring a signal (e.g., \(\sin^2 t\)) or time-variant operations like time-scaling (e.g., \(\sin 2t\)) are LTI. These operations produce new frequencies (like DC and harmonics), violating the core properties of LTI systems.

questions.question: The Fourier transform \(X(j\omega)\) of the signal is ________. \[x(t) = \frac{t}{(1+t^2)^2}\]
questions.explanation:
Consider, \[x(t) = e^{-|t|}\] by taking Fourier transform, \[e^{-|t|} \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} \frac{2}{1 + \omega^2}\] Apply differentiation in frequency, \[tx(t) \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} j \frac{d}{d\omega} X(\omega)\] \[te^{-|t|} \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} j \left[ \frac{d}{d\omega} \left( \frac{2}{1 + \omega^2} \right) \right]\] \[te^{-|t|} \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} j \left[ \frac{0 - 2(2\omega)}{(1 + \omega^2)^2} \right]\] \[te^{-|t|} \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} \frac{-4j\omega}{(1 + \omega^2)^2}\] Apply duality property, \[\frac{-4jt}{(1 + t^2)^2} \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} 2\pi(-\omega)e^{-|-\omega|}\] \[\frac{t}{(1 + t^2)^2} \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} \frac{-2\pi\omega e^{-|\omega|}}{-4j}\] \[\frac{t}{(1 + t^2)^2} \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} \boxed{\frac{\pi}{2j} \omega e^{-|\omega|}}\] \[\boxed{\text{A) $\frac{\pi}{2j}\omega e^{-|\omega|}$}}\]
Key points
  • Standard Pair: \(\mathcal{F}\{e^{-a|t|}\} = \frac{2a}{a^2 + \omega^2}\).
  • Differentiation in Frequency: Multiplication by \(t\) in the time domain corresponds to differentiation in the frequency domain: \(t x(t) \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} j \frac{d}{d\omega} X(\omega)\).
  • Duality Property: If \(x(t) \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} X(\omega)\), then \(X(t) \stackrel{F.T}{\longleftrightarrow} 2\pi x(-\omega)\).

questions.question: For a vector \(\overline{x} = [x[0], x[1], \dots, x[7]]\), the 8-point discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is denoted by \(\overline{X} = \text{DFT}(\overline{x}) = [X[0], X[1], \dots, X[7]]\), where \[X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{7} x[n] \exp \left(-j\frac{2\pi}{8}nk\right).\] Here, \(j = \sqrt{-1}\). If \(\overline{x} = [1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0]\) and \(\overline{y} = \text{DFT}(\text{DFT}(\overline{x}))\), then the value of \(y[0]\) is ________ (rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation:
The sequence \(\overline{x}\) has a length of \(N = 8\), and its elements are given by the vector: \[\overline{x} = [1, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0]\] From this, we can identify that the first element is \(x[0] = 1\). We are given \(\overline{y} = \text{DFT}(\text{DFT}(\overline{x}))\) and need to evaluate \(y[0]\). According to the duality property of the Discrete Fourier Transform, applying the DFT operator twice to an \(N\)-point sequence \(x[n]\) results in a time-reversed and scaled version of the original sequence. Mathematically, this is expressed as: \[\text{DFT}(\text{DFT}(x[n])) = N \cdot x[(-n) \bmod N]\] Therefore, the elements of the new sequence \(y[n]\) are given by: \[y[n] = 8 \cdot x[(-n) \bmod 8]\] To find the specific value of \(y[0]\), we substitute \(n = 0\) into the equation: \[y[0] = 8 \cdot x[(-0) \bmod 8]\] \[y[0] = 8 \cdot x[0]\] Substituting the known value of \(x[0] = 1\): \[y[0] = 8 \cdot 1 = 8\] \[\boxed{8}\]
Key points
  • The duality property of the \(N\)-point DFT states that if \(x[n] \leftrightarrow X[k]\), then taking the DFT of the sequence \(X[n]\) yields \(N \cdot x[(-k) \bmod N]\).
  • Applying the DFT operation twice successively to a sequence yields \(\text{DFT}\{\text{DFT}\{x[n]\}\} = N \cdot x[(-n) \bmod N]\).
  • For the zero-th index (\(n=0\)), the time-reversal and modulo operations simplify entirely, making the term exactly \(N \cdot x[0]\).
Mistakes to avoid
Attempting to calculate the 8-point DFT matrix operations manually twice is a common pitfall. While it will eventually lead to the correct answer, it is extremely time-consuming and highly prone to arithmetic errors with complex exponentials. Recognizing and applying the duality property is essential for an efficient solution.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Select the correct statement(s) regarding semiconductor devices:
options: Electrons and holes are of equal density in an intrinsic semiconductor at equilibrium.
Collector region is generally more heavily doped than base region in a \(BJT\).
Total current is spatially constant in a two terminal electronic device in dark under steady-state condition.
Mobility of electrons always increases with temperature in silicon beyond \(300\) K.
questions.explanation:
For an intrinsic semiconductor at thermal equilibrium, the electron and hole concentrations are equal: \[n=p=n_i\] Hence, statement (A) is correct. In a BJT, the emitter is heavily doped, the base is lightly doped, and the collector is moderately doped. Therefore, the collector is not more heavily doped than the base, making statement (B) incorrect. Under steady-state conditions, charge cannot continuously accumulate at any point in a two-terminal device. From the continuity equation, the total current remains spatially constant. Thus, statement (C) is correct. For silicon above room temperature, lattice (phonon) scattering becomes stronger and the electron mobility generally decreases with increasing temperature. Hence, statement (D) is incorrect. \[\boxed{(A) \text{ Electrons and holes are of equal density in an
intrinsic semiconductor at equilibrium}}\] \[\boxed{(C) \text{Total current is spatially constant in a two terminal electronic device in dark under steadystate condition.}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: Consider a long rectangular bar of direct bandgap \(p\)-type semiconductor. The equilibrium hole density is \(10^{17} \text{ cm}^{-3}\) and the intrinsic carrier concentration is \(10^{10} \text{ cm}^{-3}\). Electron and hole diffusion lengths are \(2 \text{ }\mu\text{m}\) and \(1 \text{ }\mu\text{m}\), respectively. The left side of the bar \((x = 0)\) is uniformly illuminated with a laser having photon energy greater than the bandgap of the semiconductor. Excess electron-hole pairs are generated ONLY at \(x = 0\) because of the laser. The steady state electron density at \(x = 0\) is \(10^{14} \text{ cm}^{-3}\) due to laser illumination. Under these conditions and ignoring electric field, the closest approximation (among the given options) of the steady state electron density at \(x = 2 \text{ }\mu\text{m}\), is _______.
questions.explanation:
The continuity equation is given as: \[\frac{dn}{dt} = \frac{1}{q} \frac{dJ_n(x)}{dx} + G_n(x,t) - R_n(x,t)\] Since the question mentions steady-state condition, no electric field, and carrier generation only at \(x = 0\), we conclude that for \(x>0\):
  • \(Gn = 0\), because excess carriers are generated only at the illuminated surface.
  • \(E = 0\), since electric field effects are ignored.
  • \(\dfrac{dn}{dt} = 0\) due to steady-state condition.
Thus the continuity equation becomes: \[0 = \frac{1}{q} \frac{dJ_n(x)}{dx} + G_n(x) - R_n(x)\] The electron current density \(J_n(x)\) is given as: \[J_n(x) = q\mu _nE + qD_n \frac{dn}{dx}\] Substituting \(J_n(x)\) into the continuity equation, we get: \[0= \mu _n n \frac{dE}{dx} + \mu _n E \frac{dn}{dx} + G_n(x) - Rn(x) + Dn \frac{d^2n}{dx^2}\] Given : Electric field is ignored, therefore \(E = 0\) and \(\dfrac{dE}{dx} = 0\). \[0 = 0+0+0-R_n+Dn \frac{d^2n}{dx^2}\] \[R_n = Dn \frac{d^2n}{dx^2}\] Recombination relation for excess minority carriers is given as: \[R_n = \frac{\Delta n}{\tau_n}\] Equating both equations, we get: \[\frac{\Delta n}{\tau_n} = Dn \frac{d^2n}{dx^2}\] Using \(L_n = \sqrt{D_n \tau _n}\) , \[\frac{d^2n}{dx^2} = \frac{\Delta n}{L_n^2}\] Solving this differential equation gives: \[\Delta n(x) = \Delta n (0) exp \left(- \frac{x}{L_n} \right)\] [figure unavailable] Substituting at \(x=2 \mu m\): \[\Delta n(2 \mu m) = 10^{14} exp (-1) = 0.37 \times 10^{14} \text{ cm} ^{-3}\] \[\boxed{(A) \text{ } 0.37 \times 10^{14} \text{ cm} ^{-3}}\]

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: In a non-degenerate bulk semiconductor with electron density \(n = 10^{16}\) \(cm^{-3}\), the value of \(E_C - E_{F_n} = 200\) \(meV\), where \(E_C\) and \(E_{F_n}\) denote the bottom of the conduction band energy and electron Fermi level energy, respectively. Assume thermal voltage as \(26\) \(meV\) and the intrinsic carrier concentration is \(10^{10}\) \(cm^{-3}\). For \(n = 0.5 \times 10^{16}\) \(cm^{-3}\), the closest approximation of the value of \((E_C - E_{F_n})\), among the given options, is ____
questions.explanation:
The objective is to find the energy difference \(E_{c} - E_{fn}\). The relationship between the conduction band energy level \(E_{C}\), Fermi level \(E_{F}\), and electron concentration \(n\) is given by: \[E_{C} - E_{F} = kT \ln \left( \frac{N_{c}}{n} \right)\] For two different doping concentrations \(n_{1}\) and \(n_{2}\), we have: \[E_{C} - E_{F1} = kT \ln \left( \frac{N_{c}}{n_{1}} \right) \tag{i}\] \[E_{C} - E_{F2} = kT \ln \left( \frac{N_{c}}{n_{2}} \right) \tag{ii}\] Subtracting equation (ii) from equation (i): \[(E_{C} - E_{F1}) - (E_{C} - E_{F2}) = kT \ln \left( \frac{\frac{N_{c}}{n_{1}}}{\frac{N_{c}}{n_{2}}} \right) = kT \ln \left( \frac{n_{2}}{n_{1}} \right)\] Substituting the given values (\(E_{C} - E_{F1} = 200\,\text{meV}\), \(kT = 26\,\text{meV}\), \(n_{1} = 1 \times 10^{16}\), and \(n_{2} = 0.5 \times 10^{16}\)): \[200\,\text{meV} - (E_{C} - E_{F2}) = 26\,\text{meV} \times \ln \left( \frac{0.5 \times 10^{16}}{1 \times 10^{16}} \right)\] \[200\,\text{meV} - (E_{C} - E_{F2}) = 26\,\text{meV} \times \ln(0.5) \approx -18\,\text{meV}\] \[E_{C} - E_{F2} = 200 + 18 = 218\,\text{meV}\] \[\boxed{(C) \text{ } 218 \text{ meV}}\]
Key points
  • As the electron concentration \(n\) decreases, the Fermi level moves further away from the conduction band edge.

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: A p-type semiconductor with zero electric field is under illumination (low level injection) in steady-state condition. Excess minority carrier density is zero at \(x = \pm 2l_n\), where \(l_n = 10^{-4} \text{ cm}\) is the diffusion length of electrons. Assume electronic charge, \(q = -1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}\). The profiles of photo-generation rate of carriers and the recombination rate of excess minority carriers (\(R\)) are shown. Under these conditions, the magnitude of the current density due to the photo-generated electrons at \(x = \pm 2l_n\) is ___ \(\text{mA/cm}^2\) (Rounded off to two decimal places). [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] Region 1: \(0 < x < l_n\) From the continuity equation at steady state (\(\frac{dn}{dt} = 0\)): \[0 = \frac{1}{q} \frac{dJ_n(x)}{dx} + G_n(x) - R_n(x)\] \[D_n \dfrac{d^2 \Delta n(x)}{dx^2} + G_n(x) - R_n(x) = 0\] Given \(G_n(x) = 10^{20}\) and \(R_n(x) = 10^{20} e^{-x/l_n}\), we have: \[\dfrac{d^2 \Delta n(x)}{dx^2} = \dfrac{10^{20}}{D_n} \left[ e^{-x/l_n} - 1 \right]\] Integrating once: \[\dfrac{d \Delta n(x)}{dx} = \dfrac{10^{20}}{D_n} \left[ -l_n e^{-x/l_n} - x + C \right]\] Using boundary condition at \(x = 0\): \(\left. \dfrac{d \Delta n(x)}{dx} \right|_{x=0} = 0\) \[\dfrac{10^{20}}{D_n} \left[ -l_n(1) - 0 + C \right] = 0 \implies C = l_n\] \[\therefore \dfrac{d \Delta n(x)}{dx} = \dfrac{10^{20}}{D_n} \left[ l_n (1 - e^{-x/l_n}) - x \right] , \text{ for } 0 < x < l_n\] Region 2: \(l_n < x < 2l_n\) Here \(R = G = 0\), so \(\Delta n(x)\) is linear, and current density \(J_n\) is constant. Matching slopes at \(x = l_n\): \[\text{Slope} = \left. \dfrac{d \Delta n(x)}{dx} \right|_{x=l_n} = \dfrac{10^{20}}{D_n} \left[ l_n (1 - e^{-1}) - l_n \right] = \dfrac{-10^{20} l_n e^{-1}}{D_n}\] Current density at \(x = \pm 2l_n\): \[J_n(x = \pm 2l_n) = q D_n \left. \dfrac{d \Delta n(x)}{dx} \right|_{x=2l_n} = -q 10^{20} l_n e^{-1}\] Using given values \(l_n = 10^{-4}\,\text{cm}\): \[|J_n| = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 10^{20} \times 10^{-4} \times e^{-1} \,\text{A/cm}^2\] \[|J_n| = 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.3678 \,\text{A/cm}^2 = 0.5886\,\text{mA/cm}^2\] \[\boxed{0.59}\]
Key points
  • Continuity Equation : \(D_n \dfrac{d^2 \Delta n(x)}{dx^2} + G_n(x) - R_n(x) = \dfrac{dn}{dt}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not use the Recombination formula \(R = \dfrac{\Delta n(x)}{\tau_n}\) since \(\tau_n\) is not given.
  • Don't forget to match the boundary conditions (slope continuity) at \(x = l_n\).

questions.subject: electronic-devices-circuits
questions.question: An ideal MOS capacitor (p-type semiconductor) is shown in the figure. The MOS capacitor is under strong inversion with \(V_G = 2\,\text{V}\). The corresponding inversion charge density \(Q_{IN}\) is \(2.2\,\mu\text{C/cm}^2\). Assume oxide capacitance per unit area as \(C_{OX} = 1.7\,\mu\text{F/cm}^2\). For \(V_G = 4\,\text{V}\), the value of \(Q_{IN}\) is ____ \(\mu\text{C/cm}^2\) (rounded off to one decimal place). [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
The inversion charge density is given by: \[Q_{in} = C_{ox}(V_G - V_T)\] Rearranging to find \(V_T\) using the known condition \(Q_{in} = -2.2\,\mu\text{C/cm}^2\) at \(V_G = 2\,\text{V}\): \[\frac{Q_{in}}{C_{ox}} = V_G - V_T\] \[V_T = V_G - \frac{Q_{in}}{C_{ox}} = 2 - \frac{2.2}{1.7} = 2 - 1.294\] \[V_T = 0.706\,\text{V}\] Now, computing \(Q_{in}\) at \(V_G = 4\,\text{V}\): \[Q_{in} = C_{ox}(V_G - V_T) = 1.7 \times 10^{-6} \times (4 - 0.706)\] \[Q_{in} = 1.7 \times 10^{-6} \times 3.294 = 5.5998\,\mu\text{C/cm}^2\] \[\boxed{5.6}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Confirm that \(V_G > V_T\) before applying the inversion charge formula; if \(V_G \leq V_T\) the device is not in inversion.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: A circuit and the characteristics of the diode (D) in it are shown. The ratio of the minimum to the maximum small signal voltage gain \(\dfrac{\partial V_{out}}{\partial V_{in}}\) is (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
When diode is OFF: \[V_{out} = 4I\] \[V_{in} = 6I\] \[A_{v} = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}\] When diode is ON, voltage drop across diode is \(0.7\,\text{V}\). \[V_{o} = 0.7 + (2\,\text{k}\Omega)I\] \[V_{in} = 0.7 + (4\,\text{k}\Omega)I\] \[I = \frac{V_{o} - 0.7}{2\,\text{k}\Omega}\] \[V_{in} = 0.7 + (4\,\text{k}\Omega) \cdot \frac{(V_{o} - 0.7)}{(2\,\text{k}\Omega)} = 0.7 + 2V_{o} - 1.4\] \[V_{o} = \frac{V_{in} + 0.7}{2}\] \[A_{v}' = \frac{\partial V_{o}}{\partial V_{in}} = \frac{1}{2}\] Maximum voltage gain, \(A_{v} = \frac{2}{3}\) and Minimum voltage gain, \(A_{v}' = \frac{1}{2}\) \[\boxed{\frac{(\partial V_{out} / \partial V_{in})_{\text{min}}}{(\partial V_{out} / \partial V_{in})_{\text{max}}} = \frac{A_{v}'}{A_{v}} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{3}{2} = \frac{3}{4} = 0.75}\]
Key points
  • From the graph the cut-in voltage of the diode is 0.7 V.
  • When the diode is OFF, the circuit behaves as a simple linear resistive divider.
  • During AC analysis DC voltage sources must be short circuited.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Not short circuiting the 0.7 V source while finding gain.

questions.question: Consider the CMOS circuit shown in the figure (substrates are connected to their respective sources). The gate width (\(W\)) to gate length (\(L\)) ratios \(\left(\dfrac{W}{L}\right)\) of the transistors are as shown. Both the transistors have the same gate oxide capacitance per unit area. For the \(p\)MOSFET, the threshold voltage is \(-1 \text{ V}\) and the mobility of holes is \(40 \dfrac{\text{cm}^2}{\text{V.s}}\). For the \(n\)MOSFET, the threshold voltage is \(1 \text{ V}\) and the mobility of electrons is \(300 \dfrac{\text{cm}^2}{\text{V.s}}\). The steady state output voltage \(V_o\) is _________.
questions.explanation:
Concept: MOSFET is in saturation region when \[V_{GS} > V_{th}\] \[V_{DS} > V_{GS} - V_{th}\] The current equation for a MOSFET in the saturation region is given by: \[I_D = \frac{1}{2} \mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} (V_{GS} - V_{th})^2\] \[I_D = \frac{K_n}{2} (V_{GS} - V_{th})^2\] Calculation: Both MOSFETs are in saturation because drain is shorted to Gate and they both are in series so same current flows through them. \[I_{DSN} = I_{SDP}\] \[\frac{\mu_n C_{ox}}{2} \times \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_N (V_{GSN} - V_{TN})^2 = \frac{\mu_p C_{ox}}{2} \left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_P (V_{SGP} - |V_{TP}|)^2\] \[300 \times 1 (V_0 - 1)^2 = 40 \times 5(4 - V_0 - 1)^2\] \[3(V_0^2 + 1 - 2V_0) = 2(9 + V_0^2 - 6V_0)\] \[\Rightarrow V_0^2 + 6V_0 - 15 = 0\] \[V_0 = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{36 + 4 \times 15}}{2} = \frac{-6 \pm \sqrt{96}}{2}\] \[V_0 = 1.898\,\text{V}, -7.89\,\text{V}\] \(V_0\) cannot be negative because \(V_0\) should lie between \(0\) and \(4\,\text{V}\). So, \(V_0 = 1.898\,\text{V} \text{ (Less than 2 V)}\) \[\boxed{\text{(C)}\quad \text{less than }2\,\text{V}}\]
Key points
  • A diode-connected MOSFET (Drain shorted to Gate) is always in saturation if \(V_{GS} > V_{th}\), because \(V_{DS} = V_{GS}\), which strictly satisfies the saturation condition \(V_{DS} \ge V_{GS} - V_{th}\).

questions.question: Consider the circuit shown with an ideal long channel \(n\)MOSFET (enhancement-mode, substrate is connected to the source). The transistor is appropriately biased in the saturation region with \(V_{GG}\) and \(V_{DD}\) such that it acts as a linear amplifier. \(v_i\) is the small-signal ac input voltage. \(v_A\) and \(v_B\) represent the small-signal voltages at the nodes A and B, respectively. The value of \(\dfrac{v_A}{v_B}\) is _________ (rounded off to one decimal place).
questions.explanation: AC equivalent circuit of the given figure by (i) All capacitors are short circuited. (ii) All DC voltage sources are replaced by short circuit. (iii) All DC current sources are replaced by open circuit. Small signal equivalent circuit is shown below, Voltage at \(A\), \[v_A = -R_D g_m V_{gs} \quad \dots(\text{i})\] Voltage at \(B\), \[v_B = R_s g_m V_{gs} \quad \dots(\text{ii})\] Thus, \[\frac{v_A}{v_B} = \frac{-R_D g_m V_{gs}}{R_s g_m V_{gs}} = \frac{-R_D}{R_s} = \frac{-4}{2} = -2\] \[\boxed{\frac{v_A}{v_B}=-2}\]

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: Consider an ideal long channel \(n\)MOSFET (enhancement-mode) with gate length \(10\,\mu\text{m}\) and width \(100\,\mu\text{m}\). The product of electron mobility (\(\mu_n\)) and oxide capacitance per unit area (\(C_{OX}\)) is \(\mu_nC_{OX} = 1\,\text{mA/V}^2\). The threshold voltage of the transistor is \(1\,\text{V}\). For a gate-to-source voltage \(V_{GS} = [2 - \sin(2t)]\,\text{V}\) and drain-to-source voltage \(V_{DS} = 1\,\text{V}\) (substrate connected to the source), the maximum value of the drain-to-source current is _________.
questions.explanation:
Given, \[L = 10\,\mu\text{m} ,\quad W = 100\,\mu\text{m} , \quad \mu_n C_{ox} = 1\,\text{mA/V}^2 , \quad V_T = 1\,\text{V} , \quad V_{DS} = 1\,\text{V} , \quad V_{GS} = [2 - \sin(2t)]\,\text{V}\] The maximum and minimum values of gate-to-source voltage are: \[V_{GS(\max)} = 3\,\text{V} \text{ and } V_{GS(\min)} = 1\,\text{V}\] To find the maximum drain current, we use \(V_{GS(\max)} = 3\,\text{V}\). Let's check the region of operation at maximum \(V_{GS}\): \[V_{GS(\max)} - V_T = 3 - 1 = 2\,\text{V}\] Since \(V_{DS} = 1\,\text{V}\), we have \(V_{DS} < (V_{GS(\max)} - V_T)\). Here, \(V_{DS} > (V_{GS} - V_T)\) condition will not be satisfied. Hence, nMOSFET is in Linear region. The maximum drain current is given by the linear region equation: \[I_{D_{\max}} = \mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} \left[ (V_{GS(\max)} - V_T)V_{DS} - \frac{1}{2}V_{DS}^2 \right]\] \[I_{D_{\max}} = 1\,\text{mA/V}^2 \times 10 \left[ (3 - 1)1 - \frac{1}{2} \times 1^2 \right]\] \[I_{D_{\max}} = 10[1.5]\,\text{mA} = 15\,\text{mA}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)}\quad 15\,\text{mA}}\]
Key points
  • Before calculating the current, it is crucial to verify the region of operation using the condition \(V_{DS} < V_{GS} - V_T\) for the linear (triode) region and \(V_{DS} \ge V_{GS} - V_T\) for the saturation region.
  • The drain current equation for an nMOSFET operating in the linear region is \(I_D = \mu_n C_{ox} \frac{W}{L} \left[ (V_{GS} - V_T)V_{DS} - \frac{1}{2}V_{DS}^2 \right]\).

questions.question: For the following circuit with an ideal OPAMP, the difference between the maximum and the minimum values of the capacitor voltage (\(V_c\)) is ________.
questions.explanation:
The given circuit is an astable multivibrator/free running oscillator. Case 1 : When \(V_0 = 15\,\text{V}\), \(D_1\) is ON and \(D_2\) is OFF then above circuit becomes as, Apply voltage division rule to calculate \(V^+\), \[V^+ = \frac{R \times V_0}{2R + R} = \frac{15 \times R}{3R} = \frac{15}{3} = 5\,\text{V}\] Maximum voltage across capacitor is (i.e. capacitor charged upto \(V_{UTP} = V^+\)), \[[V_c(t)]_{\text{max}} = 5\,\text{V} = V_{UTP}\] Case 2 : When \(V_0 = -12\,\text{V}\), \(D_1\) is OFF and \(D_2\) is ON, then above circuit becomes as, Applying voltage division rule to calculate \(V^+\), So, \[V^+ = V_{out} \times \frac{2R}{2R + R} = \frac{-12}{3} \times 2 = -8\,\text{V}\] Minimum capacitor voltage is (i.e. capacitor charged upto \(V_{LTP} = V^+\)), \[[V_c(t)]_{\text{min}} = -8\,\text{V} = V_{LTP}\] Thus, \[V_{c\,\text{max}} - V_{c\,\text{min}} = 5 - (-8) = 13\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{\text{(C)\quad 13 V}}\]
Key points
  • Astable Multivibrator: A circuit using an operational amplifier with positive feedback that continuously toggles between its positive and negative saturation states without external triggering.
  • Threshold Voltages: The upper threshold point (\(V_{UTP}\)) and lower threshold point (\(V_{LTP}\)) establish the boundaries for the capacitor's voltage limits.

questions.subject: analog-electronics
questions.question: A circuit with an ideal OPAMP is shown. The Bode plot for the magnitude (in dB) of the gain transfer function (\(A_V(j\omega) = V_{out}(j\omega)/V_{in}(j\omega)\)) of the circuit is also provided (here, \(\omega\) is the angular frequency in rad/s). The values of \(R\) and \(C\) are _____________.
questions.explanation:
The given Op-Amp circuit is shown below, The given Op-Amp circuit is first order active low pass filter, so low frequency (\(\omega = 0\)) gain of given low pass filter is, The above Op-Amp circuit becomes as non-inverting closed loop Op-Amp, so gain (\(A_V\)) is, \[A_V = \left[ 1 + \frac{R}{1} \right] = 1 + R \quad \dots\text{(i)}\] The \(3\text{-dB}\) cut-off frequency of given low pass filter circuit is, \[\omega_{3dB} = \frac{1}{R_1C}\,\text{rad/sec} \quad \dots\text{(ii)}\] According to given bode magnitude plot, Low frequency (\(\omega = 0\)) gain from bode magnitude plot is, \[12\,\text{dB} = 20\log_{10}(A_V)\] \[A_V = 10^{\left[\dfrac{12}{20}\right]}\] \[1 + R = 4\] \[R = 3\,\text{k}\Omega\] The \(3\text{-dB}\) frequency from bode magnitude plot, \[\log_{10} \omega_{3dB} = 3\] \[\omega_{3dB} = 10^3\] \[\omega_{3dB} = 1000\,\text{rad/sec}\] Thus, \[\omega_{3dB} = \frac{1}{R_1C} = 1000\] \[C = \frac{1}{1000 R_1} = \frac{1}{1000 \times 1000} = 1\,\mu\text{F}\] \[\boxed{\text{(A)\quad} R = 3~\text{k}\Omega,\; C = 1~\mu\text{F}}\]
Key points
  • Active Low-Pass Filter: The circuit consists of a passive RC low-pass network at the input of a non-inverting operational amplifier, isolating the filter from the load and providing voltage gain.
  • DC Gain Evaluation: At low frequencies (\(\omega \to 0\)), the capacitor acts as an open circuit. The gain is solely determined by the non-inverting amplifier configuration: \(A_V = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_i}\).
  • Bode Plot Analysis: The flat low-frequency magnitude gives the DC gain in decibels (\(20\log_{10}|A_V|\)), while the corner frequency (where the gain falls by \(3\,\text{dB}\)) identifies the pole of the RC network (\(\omega_{3dB} = \frac{1}{RC}\)).

The Boolean inputs ‘\(0\)’ and ‘\(1\)’ are also available separately. Using instances of only D gates and inputs ‘\(0\)’ and ‘\(1\)’, (select the correct option(s)).
questions.explanation:
Given: A Boolean gate (\(D\)) where the output \(Y\) is related to the inputs \(A\) and \(B\) as, \(Y = A + \overline{B}\). REMEMBER: If any logic circuit can give "AND" or "OR" (Either ONE of them) and "NOT" together then that circuit can be used as universal Gate [with the condition that "1" and "0" are present]. To Prove, we will implement NOR gate with the given gate as NOR is a known universal gate so if that is implemented we can implement all functions through it. (A) NAND logic can be implemented
(C) NOR logic can be implemented

If any logic circuit can give "AND" or "OR"(Either ONE of them) and "NOT" together then that circuit can be used as universal Gate (with the condition that "1" and "0" are present).Thus the following functions are sufficient to implement any Boolean Expression: NAND , NOR , AND+NOT , OR+NOT , AND+OR+NOT .

questions.ref: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra Q2
questions.question: Select the Boolean function(s) equivalent to \(x + yz\), where \(x, y,\) and \(z\) are Boolean variables, and \(+\) denotes logical OR operation.
questions.explanation:
Method 1
Choosing from options: From option (A): & From option (B): & From option (C): & From option (D): \(x + z + xy\) & \((x + y)(x + z)\) & \(x + xy + yz\) & \(x + xz + xy\) \(x(1 + y) + z\) & \(x + xz + yx + yz\) & \(x(1 + y) + yz\) & \(x(1 + z + y)\) \(= x + z\) & \(= x + yz\) & \(= x + yz\) & \(= x\) (A) is incorrect. & (B) is correct. & (C) is correct. & (D) is incorrect. Hence, the correct options are (B) and (C).

Given: \((x + yz) \dots(i)\) From Boolean algebra distributive law: \[A + BC = (A + B)(A + C)\] So, equation (i) can be written as: \[\underline{x + yz = (x + y)(x + z)}\] Again, using the identity \(A + AB = A\): \[A + BC = A(1 + B) + BC = A + AB + BC\] So, equation (i) can also be written as: \[\underline{x + yz = x + xy + yz}\]

questions.question: Consider the 2-bit multiplexer (MUX) shown in the figure. For OUTPUT to be the XOR of C and D, the values for \(A_0, A_1, A_2,\) and \(A_3\) are .
questions.explanation:
The given circuit is a \(4 \times 1\) Multiplexer (MUX) with inputs and selection lines as shown in the diagram. The general characteristic equation for the output \(F\) of a \(4 \times 1\) MUX is: \[F = \overline{S}_1\overline{S}_0A_0 + \overline{S}_1S_0A_1 + S_1\overline{S}_0A_2 + S_1S_0A_3 \dots (i)\] From the given figure:
  • Selection lines: \(S_1 = C\) and \(S_0 = D\)
  • Inputs: \(A_0, A_1, A_2, A_3\)
Substituting the selection lines into equation \((i)\): \[F = \overline{C}\overline{D}A_0 + \overline{C}DA_1 + C\overline{D}A_2 + CDA_3\] The goal is to implement the XOR logic function: \[F = C \oplus D = \overline{C}D + C\overline{D}\] Comparing the XOR expression with the MUX output expression:
  • To get the \(\overline{C}D\) term, we must set \(A_1 = 1\).
  • To get the \(C\overline{D}\) term, we must set \(A_2 = 1\).
  • The terms \(\overline{C}\overline{D}\) and \(CD\) are not present in the XOR function, so we must set \(A_0 = 0\) and \(A_3 = 0\).
Thus, the required input values are \(A_0 = 0\), \(A_1 = 1\), \(A_2 = 1\), and \(A_3 = 0\). Hence, the correct option is (C). \[\boxed{(C)A_0 = 0, A_1 = 1, A_2 = 1, A_3 = 0}\]
Key points
  • A \(4 \times 1\) MUX can implement any \(2\)-variable boolean function directly by connecting inputs to logic \(0\) or \(1\) according to the truth table of the required function.
  • For a MUX acting as a function generator, the inputs \(A_n\) correspond to the truth table output values for the minterms addressed by the selection lines.

questions.question: For the circuit shown, the clock frequency is \(f_0\) and the duty cycle is 25%. For the signal at the \(Q\) output of the Flip-Flop, .
options: frequency is \(f_0/4\) and duty cycle is 50%
frequency is \(f_0/4\) and duty cycle is 25%
frequency is \(f_0/2\) and duty cycle is 50%
frequency is \(f_0\) and duty cycle is 25%
questions.explanation:
For an edge-triggered counter and latch, the circuit responds only to the active clock edge (rising edge in this case). The duty cycle of the clock pulse is irrelevant to the triggering mechanism; thus, a 25% duty cycle does not change the state transition timing compared to a 50% duty cycle. // The timing diagram of the output will be as follows Analyzing the timing diagram provided:
  • The clock has a time period \(T\).
  • The LSB of the counter toggles at every rising clock edge, resulting in a period of \(2T\).
  • Since \(J = K = \text{LSB}\), the inputs to the JK flip-flop change according to the previous value of the LSB at each clock edge.
  • Due to the toggle nature when \(J=K=1\) and hold when \(J=K=0\), the output \(Q^{+}\) transitions such that its complete cycle spans four clock periods.
The time period of the output signal (\(T'\)) is: \[T' = 4T\]
Consequently, the output frequency (\(f_{o}'\)) is related to the input clock frequency (\(f_{o}\)) as: \[\boxed{\text{(A) frequency is $f_0/4$ and duty cycle is 50\%}}\] Furthermore, as observed from the waveform, the output \(Q^{+}\) maintains a 50% duty cycle (High for \(2T\), Low for \(2T\)) despite the clock having only a 25% duty cycle.
Key points
  • Edge Triggering: In synchronous circuits, state changes occur only at the clock transition, making the pulse width (duty cycle) irrelevant.
  • Frequency Division: A flip-flop acting as a toggle (T-type or JK with \(J=K=1\)) divides the frequency of its trigger signal by 2.

questions.question: A state transition diagram with states \(A, B,\) and \(C\), and transition probabilities \(p_1, p_2, \dots, p_7\) is shown in the figure (e.g., \(p_1\) denotes the probability of transition from state \(A\) to \(B\)). For this state diagram, select the statement(s) which is/are universally true.
questions.explanation:
Based on the provided state transition diagram, we analyze the transition probabilities from each state. The sum of all outgoing transition probabilities from any given state must equal 1. Case 1: Transitions from A
From state \(A\), the system can transition to state \(B\) (with probability \(p_{1}\)), state \(C\) (with probability \(p_{4}\)), or remain in state \(A\) (with probability \(p_{7}\)). \[p_{1} + p_{4} + p_{7} = 1\] Case 2: Transitions from B
From state \(B\), the system can transition to state \(A\) (with probability \(p_{3}\)) or remain in state \(B\) (with probability \(p_{2}\)). \[p_{2} + p_{3} = 1\] Case 3: Transitions C
From state \(C\), the system can transition to state \(A\) (with probability \(p_{6}\)) or remain in state \(C\) (with probability \(p_{5}\)). \[p_{5} + p_{6} = 1\] Comparing the results from Case 2 and Case 3: \[p_{2} + p_{3} = p_{5} + p_{6} = 1\] Thus, the relationships \[p_{1} + p_{4} + p_{7} = 1\] and \(p_{2} + p_{3} = p_{5} + p_{6}\) are valid based on the fundamental properties of state transition diagrams.
(A) \(p_2 + p_3 = p_5 + p_6\)
(C) \(p_1 + p_4 + p_7 = 1\)
Key points
  • In any state transition diagram or Markov chain, the sum of probabilities for all outgoing edges from a single node must be exactly 1.
  • Self-loops must be included in the summation of outgoing probabilities.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not confuse incoming transitions with outgoing transitions; only outgoing transitions contribute to the probability sum of 1 for a specific state.

questions.question: Two linear time-invariant systems with transfer functions \[G_1(s) = \frac{10}{s^2 + s + 1} \text{ and } G_2(s) = \frac{10}{s^2 + s\sqrt{10} + 10}\] have unit step responses \(y_1(t)\) and \(y_2(t)\), respectively. Which of the following statements is/are true?
options: \(y_1(t)\) and \(y_2(t)\) have the same percentage peak overshoot.
\(y_1(t)\) and \(y_2(t)\) have the same steady-state value.
\(y_1(t)\) and \(y_2(t)\) have the same damped frequency of oscillation.
\(y_1(t)\) and \(y_2(t)\) have the same \(2\%\) settling time.
questions.explanation:
For system 1: \[G_{1}(s) = \frac{10}{s^{2} + s + 1}\] Characteristic equation: \(s^{2} + s + 1 = 0\) Comparing with standard eqn: \(s^{2} + 2\xi\omega_{n}s + \omega_{n}^{2} = 0\) \[\omega_{n} = 1, \quad \xi = 0.5\] \[\omega_{d} = 1\sqrt{1-(0.5)^{2}} = 0.866\] Settling time (\(2\%\) criterion): \[t_{s1} = \frac{4}{\xi\omega_{n}} = \frac{4}{0.5 \times 1} = 8\,\text{sec}\] Steady-state value: \[y_{1}(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{10}{s^{2} + s + 1} = 10\] For system 2: \[G_{2}(s) = \frac{10}{s^{2} + \sqrt{10}s + 10}\] Characteristic equation: \(s^{2} + \sqrt{10}s + 10 = 0\) Comparing with standard eqn: \(s^{2} + 2\xi\omega_{n}s + \omega_{n}^{2} = 0\) \[\omega_{n} = \sqrt{10}, \quad \xi = 0.5\] \[\omega_{d} = \sqrt{10}\sqrt{1-(0.5)^{2}} = 2.739\] Settling time (\(2\%\) criterion): \[t_{s2} = \frac{4}{0.5\sqrt{10}} = 2.535\,\text{sec}\] Steady-state value: \[y_{2}(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} \frac{10}{s^{2} + \sqrt{10}s + 10} = 1\] Since the damping ratio \(\xi\) is the same (\(0.5\)) for both systems, the percentage peak overshoot (\(M_{p} = e^{-\frac{\xi\pi}{\sqrt{1-\xi^{2}}}} \times 100\%\)) is identical. \[M_{p1} = M_{p2}\] \[\boxed{(A) \ \ \text{ }y_1(t)\text{ and }y_2(t)\text{ have the same percentage peak overshoot}}\]
Key points
Steady-state value of a unit step response is given by the DC gain of the system, \(\lim_{s \to 0} G(s)\).

questions.question: The block diagram of a closed-loop control system is shown in the figure. \(R(s), Y(s)\), and \(D(s)\) are the Laplace transforms of the time-domain signals \(r(t), y(t)\), and \(d(t)\), respectively. Let the error signal be defined as \(e(t) = r(t) - y(t)\). Assuming the reference input \(r(t) = 0\) for all \(t\), the steady-state error \(e(\infty)\), due to a unit step disturbance \(d(t)\), is
questions.explanation: \(R(s) = 0\), So the given above block diagram can be reduced as below, Thus, the transfer function of the reduced block diagram is, \[\frac{Y(s)}{D(s)} = \frac{\frac{1}{s(s+10)}}{1 + \frac{10}{s(s+10)}} = \frac{1}{s(s+10) + 10} \quad \dots(\text{i})\] According to the question, the error signal is defined as \(e(t) = r(t) - y(t)\). Since \(r(t) = 0\): \[e(t) = -y(t) \implies E(s) = -Y(s)\] Substituting this into equation (i): \[-E(s) = \frac{D(s)}{s(s+10) + 10}\] Steady-state error \(e(\infty)\) under a unit step disturbance \(\left[ D(s) = \dfrac{1}{s} \right]\) is calculated using the Final Value Theorem: \[e(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} sE(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \left[ \frac{-D(s)}{s(s+10) + 10} \right ]= \lim_{s \to 0} s \left[ \frac{-\frac{1}{s}}{s(s+10) + 10} \right] = -\frac{1}{10} = -0.1\] \[\boxed{e(\infty) = -0.1}\]

questions.question: Consider an even polynomial \(p(s)\) given by \[p(s) = s^4 + 5s^2 + 4 + K ,\] where \(K\) is an unknown real parameter. The complete range of \(K\) for which \(p(s)\) has all its roots on the imaginary axis is _____.
questions.explanation:
Given \(p(s) = s^4 + 5s^2 + (4 + K)\). It is mentioned that all 4 roots lie on the imaginary axis. Hence, the \(s^3\) row is zero. The auxiliary equation is \(A(s) = s^4 + 5s^2 + (4 + K)\). The derivative \(\frac{dA(s)}{ds} = 4s^3 + 10s\) provides the coefficients to replace the zero row. \[\begin{array}{c|ccc}
s^4 & 1 & 5 & (4+K) \\
s^3 & 0 & 0 & \text{...Zero Row} \\
s^3 & 4 & 10 & \text{...Replaced Row} \\
s^2 & 2.5 & (4+K) & \\
s^1 & \frac{25-4(4+K)}{2.5} & & \\
s^0 & 4+K & & 
\end{array}\] For all roots to lie on the imaginary axis, the first column of the R-H table must be all positive: 1. \(\dfrac{25 - 16 - 4K}{2.5} > 0 \implies 9 > 4K \implies K < \frac{9}{4}\) 2. \(4 + K > 0 \implies K > -4\) \[\boxed{(A) \ \ \text{-4 < K < 9/4} }\]

questions.question: The root-locus plot of a closed-loop system with unity negative feedback and transfer function \(KG(s)\) in the forward path is shown in the figure. Note that \(K\) is varied from \(0\) to \(\infty\). Select the transfer function \(G(s)\) that results in the root-locus plot of the closed-loop system as shown in the figure.
questions.explanation:
There are 5 root-locus branches from the same point, so there are 5 real multiple poles. From the root-locus plot, the centroid is located at \(-1\). Since there are 5 branches originating from this single point on the real axis and no finite zeros are visible, it indicates 5 multiple poles at \(s = -1\). The corresponding forward path transfer function is: \[\boxed{(A)\ \ G(s) = \frac{1}{(s + 1)^{5}}}\]
Key points
  • The number of root-locus branches is equal to the number of open-loop poles (\(n\)).
  • The angles of asymptotes for \(n\) poles and \(m\) zeros are given by \(\theta = \frac{(2q+1)180^{\circ}}{n-m}\).

questions.question: Consider a closed-loop control system with unity negative feedback and \(K G(s)\) in the forward path, where the gain \(K = 2\). The complete Nyquist plot of the transfer function \(G(s)\) is shown in the figure. Note that the Nyquist contour has been chosen to have the clockwise sense. Assume \(G(s)\) has no poles on the closed right-half of the complex plane. The number of poles of the closed-loop transfer function in the closed right-half of the complex plane is .
questions.explanation:
In the question, the Nyquist plot is given for \(G(s)\). The forward path gain is \(K=2\) with unity negative feedback. Hence, the open-loop transfer function becomes \(2G(s)\) Scaling the Nyquist plot of \(G(s)\) by a factor of \(2\) enlarges the plot radially by \(2\). Therefore, the Nyquist plot for \(2G(s)\) is shown below. The problem states that \(G(s)\) has no poles in the closed right half plane. Scaling by a constant gain does not change the pole locations. Hence, the open-loop transfer function \(2G(s)\) also has no poles in the right half plane. Therefore, \(P_{+}=0\) For unity negative feedback, the characteristic equation is \[1+2G(s)=0\] The poles of the closed-loop transfer function are the zeros of the characteristic equation. Using Nyquist criterion, \[N=P_{+}-Z_{+}\] where,
  • \(N\) = net number of clockwise encirclements of \((-1,j0)\)
  • \(P_{+}\) = number of right half plane poles of characteristic equation, which is same as the poles of open loop system
  • \(Z_{+}\) = number of right half plane zeros of characteristic equation
It is given in the question that the Nyquist contour is traversed in clockwise direction. From the scaled Nyquist plot, the critical point \((-1,j0)\) is encircled twice in clockwise direction by \(2G(s)\) plot. The number of times \(2G(s)\) encircles \((-1,j0)\) is same as the number of times \(1+2G(s)=0\) encirlces origin. Hence, \[N=-2\] Substituting in Nyquist criterion, \[-2=0-Z_{+}\] \[Z_{+}=2\] Since the poles of the closed-loop transfer function are the zeros of the characteristic equation. Hence the number of closed-loop poles in RHP = 2. \[\boxed{\text{(C) }2}\]
Key points
  • Scaling the open-loop transfer function by a constant gain scales the Nyquist plot radially.
  • Multiplying by gain does not change pole locations.
  • Closed-loop poles are the zeros of the characteristic equation. And open loop poles are equal to the poles of characteristic equation.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not apply Nyquist criterion directly on the unscaled plot when gain changes.
  • Be careful with the sign convention of clockwise encirclements.
  • Do not confuse poles of open-loop transfer function with poles of closed-loop transfer function.

questions.question: Consider a real valued source whose samples are independent and identically distributed random variables with the probability density function, \(f(x)\), as shown in the figure. Consider a 1 bit quantizer that maps positive samples to value \(\alpha\) and others to value \(\beta\). If \(\alpha^*\) and \(\beta^*\) are the respective choices for \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) that minimize the mean square quantization error, then \((\alpha^* - \beta^*) = \rule{3cm}{0.4pt}\) (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: \[\text{Using the property that total area under a pdf must be equal to }1\] \[\frac{1}{2}\times2\times h+1\times h=1\] \[2h=1\] \[h=0.5\] Hence, \[f(x)=\frac{1}{4}(x+2), \qquad -2\le x\le0\] \[f(x)=0.5, \qquad 0\le x\le1\] \[\text{For }0\le x\le1,\quad x_q=\alpha \quad \text{and} \quad \theta_e=x-\alpha\] \[\text{For }-2\le x\le0,\quad x_q=\beta \quad \text{and} \quad \theta_e=x-\beta\] \[\text{Quantization noise power is minimized using mean square error criterion}\] \[N_q=E[\theta_e^2] = \int_0^1 (x-\alpha)^2\frac{1}{2}\,dx\] \[= \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{3} \left[(x-\alpha)^3\right]_0^1\] \[= \frac{1}{6} \left[(1-\alpha)^3+\alpha^3\right]\] For minimum noise power, \[\frac{dN_q}{d\alpha}=0\] \[\Rightarrow \frac{1}{6} \left[ 3(1-\alpha)^2(-1)+3\alpha^2 \right] =0\] \[3\alpha^2=3(1-\alpha)^2\] \[\alpha^2=1+\alpha^2-2\alpha\] \[2\alpha=1\] \[\boxed{ \alpha=0.5 }\] Now, \[N_q=E[\theta_e^2] = \int_{-2}^{0} (x-\beta)^2 \frac{1}{4}(x+2)\,dx\] \[= \frac{1}{4} \int_{-2}^{0} (x^2+\beta^2-2x\beta)(x+2)\,dx\] Expanding, \[= \frac{1}{4} \int_{-2}^{0} \left( x^3+\beta^2x-2x^2\beta+2x^2+2\beta^2-4x\beta \right)\,dx\] \[= \frac{1}{4} \Bigg[ \frac{1}{4}(-16) +\frac{\beta^2}{2}(-4) -\frac{2\beta}{3}(8) +\frac{2}{3}(8) +2\beta^2(2) -2\beta(-4) \Bigg]\] \[= -1-\frac{\beta^2}{2} -\frac{4\beta}{3} +\frac{4}{3} +\beta^2 +2\beta\] For minimum noise power, \[\frac{dN_q}{d\beta}=0\] \[\Rightarrow -\beta-\frac{4}{3}+2\beta+2=0\] \[\beta=\frac{4}{3}-2\] \[\boxed{ \beta=-\frac{2}{3} }\] Finally, \[\alpha-\beta = \frac{1}{2} -\left(-\frac{2}{3}\right)\] \[= \frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{3} = \frac{3+4}{6} = \frac{7}{6}\] \[\boxed{ \alpha-\beta=\frac{7}{6}\approx1.17 }\]

questions.question: A symbol stream contains alternate QPSK and \(16\)-QAM symbols. If symbols from this stream are transmitted at the rate of \(1\) mega-symbols per second, the raw (uncoded) data rate is mega-bits per second. (rounded off to one decimal place)
questions.explanation:
Given: The symbol rate is related to the bit rate by \[R_b = R_s \log_2 M\]where \[R_b = \text{Bit rate}, \qquad R_s = \text{Symbol rate}, \qquad M = \text{Modulation order}.\] Theory: Each symbol in an \(M\)-ary modulation scheme carries \(\log_2 M\) bits. Given symbol rate, \[R_s = 1~\text{Msymbol/s}.\] For QPSK: \[M = 4 = 2^2\] \[R_{b1} = R_s \log_2 4 = 1 \times 2 = 2~\text{Mbps}.\] For 16-QAM: \[M = 16 = 2^4\] \[R_{b2} = R_s \log_2 16 = 1 \times 4 = 4~\text{Mbps}.\] Since the transmitted symbol stream alternates equally between QPSK and 16-QAM symbols, the average bit rate is \[R_b = \frac{R_{b1}+R_{b2}}{2}\] \[= \frac{2+4}{2}\] \[= 3~\text{Mbps}.\] \[\boxed{R_b = 3~\text{Mbps}}\]
Key points
  • Symbol rate and bit rate are related by \[R_b = R_s \log_2 M.\]
  • Each QPSK symbol carries \[\log_2 4 = 2\] bits.
  • Each 16-QAM symbol carries \[\log_2 16 = 4\] bits.
  • When two modulation schemes occur equally often, the overall bit rate is the arithmetic mean of their individual bit rates.

questions.question: The frequency response \(H(f)\) of a linear time-invariant system has magnitude as shown in the figure. Statement I : The system is necessarily a pure delay system for inputs which are bandlimited to \(-\alpha \le f \le \alpha\). Statement II : For any wide-sense stationary input process with power spectral density \(S_X(f)\), the output power spectral density \(S_Y(f)\) obeys \(S_Y(f) = S_X(f)\) for \(-\alpha \le f \le \alpha\). [figure unavailable] Which one of the following combinations is true?
options: Statement I is correct, Statement II is correct
Statement I is correct, Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect, Statement II is correct
Statement I is incorrect, Statement II is incorrect
questions.explanation:
Given: The frequency response \(H(f)\) of a linear time-invariant system has magnitude: \[|H(f)| = \begin{cases} 1, & -\alpha \le f \le \alpha \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}\] Theory: A pure delay system with time delay \(T_d\) has the transfer function: \[H(f) = e^{-j 2 \pi f T_d}\] [figure unavailable] This requires both a constant magnitude \(|H(f)| = 1\) and a linear phase response \(\angle H(f) = -2\pi f T_d\). Knowing only the magnitude response \(|H(f)|\) is not sufficient to classify a system as a pure delay system, because any arbitrary phase response \(\angle H(f)\) can exist while keeping \(|H(f)| = 1\). For a Wide-Sense Stationary (WSS) process passed through a linear time-invariant system, the output power spectral density \(S_Y(f)\) is related to the input power spectral density \(S_X(f)\) by: \[S_Y(f) = |H(f)|^2 S_X(f)\] [figure unavailable] Analysis of Statement I: Without information about the phase response \(\angle H(f)\), we cannot guarantee that the system is a pure delay system. Thus, Statement I is not necessarily true. \[\text{Statement I is } \textbf{incorrect}.\] Analysis of Statement II: For inputs bandlimited to \(-\alpha \le f \le \alpha\), we have \(|H(f)| = 1\). Substituting this into the power spectral density formula: \[S_Y(f) = |H(f)|^2 S_X(f) = (1)^2 S_X(f) = S_X(f) \quad \text{for } -\alpha \le f \le \alpha\] \[\text{Statement II is } \textbf{correct}.\] \[\boxed{ \text{(C) Statement I is incorrect, and Statement II is correct.} }\]
Key points
  • A pure delay system \(y(t) = x(t - T_d)\) requires both constant magnitude \(|H(f)| = 1\) and linear phase response \(\angle H(f) = -2\pi f T_d\).
  • Magnitude spectrum alone does not define system behavior uniquely, as phase response can introduce phase distortion without altering \(|H(f)|\).
  • The relation between input and output Power Spectral Densities (PSD) depends solely on the squared magnitude response: \[S_Y(f) = |H(f)|^2 S_X(f)\]
  • Phase response has no effect on the output Power Spectral Density \(S_Y(f)\).

questions.question: Consider communication over a memoryless binary symmetric channel using a \((7,4)\) Hamming code. Each transmitted bit is received correctly with probability \((1-\epsilon)\), and flipped with probability \(\epsilon\). For each codeword transmission, the receiver performs minimum Hamming distance decoding, and correctly decodes the message bits if and only if the channel introduces at most one bit error. For \(\epsilon=0.1\), the probability that a transmitted codeword is decoded correctly is . (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Given: A \((7,4)\) Hamming code is used over a Binary Symmetric Channel (BSC). \[\epsilon=P(1|0)=P(0|1)=0.1\]The \((7,4)\) Hamming code can correct one bit error. Therefore, decoding is correct if the received codeword contains at most one error. Theory: For a BSC, the probability of exactly \(r\) bit errors in an \(n\)-bit codeword follows the binomial distribution \[P(r\ \text{errors}) = {}^{n}C_{r} \epsilon^r (1-\epsilon)^{n-r}.\]Since the Hamming code corrects all patterns with \(0\) or \(1\) error, \[P_{\text{correct}} = P(0\ \text{errors}) + P(1\ \text{error}).\] Probability of zero errors \[P(0\ \text{errors}) = {}^{7}C_{0} (0.1)^0 (0.9)^7\] \[= (0.9)^7\] \[= 0.4782969.\] Probability of exactly one error \[P(1\ \text{error}) = {}^{7}C_{1} \epsilon^1 (1-\epsilon)^6\] \[= {}^{7}C_{1} (0.1)^1 (0.9)^6\] \[= 7(0.1)(0.9)^6\] \[= 0.3720087.\] Probability of correct decoding \[P_{\text{correct}} = 0.4782969 + 0.3720087\] \[= 0.8503056.\] \[P_{\text{correct}} \approx 0.8503.\] \[\boxed{ P_{\text{correct}} = (0.9)^7 + 7(0.1)(0.9)^6 = 0.8503 }\]
Key points
  • For a linear block code, the notation \((n,k)\) means: \[k = \text{number of message (information) bits}\] \[n = \text{number of bits in the encoded codeword}\] \[r = n-k = \text{number of parity (redundancy) bits}\]
  • Thus, the code rate is \[R=\frac{k}{n}.\]
  • For a \((7,4)\) Hamming code, \[n=7,\qquad k=4,\qquad r=n-k=7-4=3.\]
  • Hence, every 4-bit message is encoded into a 7-bit codeword by adding 3 parity bits.
  • In general, for a Hamming code, \[n=2^{r}-1,\] \[k=2^{r}-r-1,\] \[r=n-k.\]
  • Example: \[r=3\] \[n=2^3-1=7,\] \[k=2^3-3-1=4.\]Therefore, the \((7,4)\) Hamming code contains \(4\) information bits and \(3\) parity bits.

questions.question: Consider a channel over which either symbol \(x_A\) or symbol \(x_B\) is transmitted. Let the output of the channel \(Y\) be the input to a maximum likelihood (ML) detector at the receiver. The conditional probability density functions for \(Y\) given \(x_A\) and \(x_B\) are: \[f_{Y|x_A}(y)=e^{-(y+1)}u(y+1),\] \[f_{Y|x_B}(y)=e^{(y-1)}\big(1-u(y-1)\big),\]where \(u(\cdot)\) is the standard unit step function. The probability of symbol error for this system is . (rounded off to two decimal places)
questions.explanation:
Given:
[figure unavailable] Assume both hypotheses are equally likely. For a Maximum Likelihood (ML) detector, the decision rule is based on comparing the likelihood functions: \[\text{Decide } x_{A} \text{ if } f_{Y|x_{A}}(y) > f_{Y|x_{B}}(y)\] \[\text{Decide } x_{B} \text{ if } f_{Y|x_{B}}(y) > f_{Y|x_{A}}(y)\] Given the conditional probability density functions: \[f_{Y|x_{A}}(y) = e^{-(y+1)}u(y+1)\] \[f_{Y|x_{B}}(y) = e^{(y-1)}(1 - u(y-1))\] To find the decision boundaries, we equate the two PDFs where they both exist and overlap (i.e., for \(-1 < y < 1\)): \[e^{-(y+1)} = e^{(y-1)}\] \[-(y+1) = y-1\] \[-y - 1 = y - 1 \implies 2y = 0 \implies y = 0\] Now, we determine the decision regions by analyzing the intervals based on the given functions:
  • For \(y < -1\): \(f_{Y|x_{A}}(y) = 0\) and \(f_{Y|x_{B}}(y) > 0 \implies\) Decide \(x_{B}\).
  • For \(-1 < y < 0\): \(f_{Y|x_{A}}(y) > f_{Y|x_{B}}(y) \implies\) Decide \(x_{A}\).
  • For \(0 < y < 1\): \(f_{Y|x_{B}}(y) > f_{Y|x_{A}}(y) \implies\) Decide \(x_{B}\).
  • For \(y > 1\): \(f_{Y|x_{B}}(y) = 0\) and \(f_{Y|x_{A}}(y) > 0 \implies\) Decide \(x_{A}\).
Thus, the decision regions for each symbol are: \[R_{A} \text{ (Region for } x_{A}) = (-1, 0) \cup (1, \infty)\] \[R_{B} \text{ (Region for } x_{B}) = (-\infty, -1) \cup (0, 1)\] Assuming equiprobable symbols for the overall probability of symbol error (\(P(x_{A}) = P(x_{B}) = 0.5\)), the total probability of error \(P_{e}\) is: \[P_{e} = P(x_{A})P(\text{error} | x_{A}) + P(x_{B})P(\text{error} | x_{B})\] Calculating \(P(\text{error} | x_{A})\) (which occurs when \(y\) falls in \(R_{B}\)): \[P(\text{error} | x_{A}) = \int_{R_{B}} f_{Y|x_{A}}(y) \, dy = \int_{-\infty}^{-1} 0 \, dy + \int_{0}^{1} e^{-(y+1)} \, dy\] \[P(\text{error} | x_{A}) = \left[ -e^{-(y+1)} \right]_{0}^{1} = -e^{-2} - (-e^{-1}) = e^{-1} - e^{-2}\] Calculating \(P(\text{error} | x_{B})\) (which occurs when \(y\) falls in \(R_{A}\)): \[P(\text{error} | x_{B}) = \int_{R_{A}} f_{Y|x_{B}}(y) \, dy = \int_{-1}^{0} e^{(y-1)} \, dy + \int_{1}^{\infty} 0 \, dy\] \[P(\text{error} | x_{B}) = \left[ e^{(y-1)} \right]_{-1}^{0} = e^{-1} - e^{-2}\] Therefore, the total probability of error is: \[P_{e} = 0.5(e^{-1} - e^{-2}) + 0.5(e^{-1} - e^{-2}) = e^{-1} - e^{-2}\] \[P_{e} = \frac{1}{e} - \frac{1}{e^2} \approx 0.36788 - 0.13534 = 0.23254\] Rounding off to two decimal places, we get \(0.23\). \[\boxed{0.23}\]
Key points
  • The Maximum Likelihood (ML) rule minimizes the probability of error by deciding on the symbol that maximizes the likelihood function \(f_{Y|X}(y)\).
  • The probability of error for a specific transmitted symbol is the area under its conditional PDF curve in the regions assigned to other symbols.
  • \(P_{e} = \sum P(x_{i}) \int_{y \notin R_{i}} f_{Y|x_{i}}(y) \, dy\).
Mistakes to avoid
A common mistake is assuming standard single-threshold decision regions (e.g., \(y > 0 \implies x_{A}\) and \(y < 0 \implies x_{B}\)). Always evaluate the PDFs across the entire range from \(-\infty\) to \(\infty\) because the presence of step functions \(u(\cdot)\) can create disjoint decision regions, as seen in this problem.

questions.question: The transition diagram of a discrete memoryless channel with three input symbols and three output symbols is shown below. [figure unavailable] The transition probabilities are as marked.The parameter \(\alpha\) lies in the interval \([0.25,1]\). The value of \(\alpha\) for which the capacity of this channel is maximized is (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Theory:Channel capacity is the maximum mutual information between the input and output. For a strongly symmetric channel, capacity is obtained using a uniform input distribution. The channel transition matrix is \[P(Y|X)= \begin{bmatrix} 1-\alpha & \alpha & 0\\ 0 & 1-\alpha & \alpha\\ \alpha & 0 & 1-\alpha \end{bmatrix}.\]Since each row is a permutation of the others and all column sums are equal, the channel is strongly symmetric. Therefore, \[C = \log_2 3 - H\!\left(\frac{Y}{X}\right).\]The conditional entropy of any row is \[H\!\left(\frac{Y}{X}\right) = -(1-\alpha)\log_2(1-\alpha) -\alpha\log_2\alpha.\]Hence, \[C = \log_2 3 + (1-\alpha)\log_2(1-\alpha) + \alpha\log_2\alpha.\]\[H\!\left(\frac{Y}{X}\right) = -\alpha\log_2\alpha -(1-\alpha)\log_2(1-\alpha)\] \[C = \log_2 3 + \alpha\log_2\alpha + (1-\alpha)\log_2(1-\alpha)\] \[C=f(\alpha)\]For maximum/minimum points, \[\frac{dC}{d\alpha}=0\] \[\frac{d}{d\alpha} \left[ \alpha\log_2\alpha + (1-\alpha)\log_2(1-\alpha) \right] =0\]Using \[\frac{d}{d\alpha} \big(\alpha\ln\alpha\big) = \ln\alpha+1,\]and \[\frac{d}{d\alpha} \big((1-\alpha)\ln(1-\alpha)\big) = -\ln(1-\alpha)-1,\]we get \[\ln\alpha+1-\ln(1-\alpha)-1=0\] \[\ln\alpha-\ln(1-\alpha)=0\] \[\ln\!\left(\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}\right)=0\] \[\frac{\alpha}{1-\alpha}=1\] \[\alpha=1-\alpha\] \[2\alpha=1\] \[\boxed{\alpha=\frac{1}{2}}\] [figure unavailable] Thus, \(\alpha=\frac{1}{2}\) is the stationary point and corresponds to the minimum value of \(C\). Since \[\alpha\in[0.25,1],\]the maximum capacity occurs at the boundary point \[\boxed{\alpha=1}.\]

questions.question: Let \(H(X)\) denote the entropy of a discrete random variable \(X\) taking \(K\) possible distinct real values.Which of the following statements is/are necessarily true?
questions.explanation:
Theory: If \(Y=g(X)\) is a one-to-one transformation of a discrete random variable \(X\), then entropy is preserved: \[H(Y)=H(X).\]Also, for a discrete random variable having \(K\) possible values, \[H(X)\leq \log_2 K,\]with equality when all outcomes are equiprobable. Option (A): Since \(X\) can take at most \(K\) distinct values, \[H(X)\leq \log_2 K.\]Hence, option (A) is true. Option (B): The transformation \[Y=2X\] is one-to-one. Therefore, \[H(2X)=H(X).\]Hence, \[H(X)\leq H(2X)\]is true. Option (C): The transformation \[Y=X^2\]need not be one-to-one. Consider \[P(X=-1)=\frac14,\qquad P(X=0)=\frac12,\qquad P(X=1)=\frac14.\]Then \[X^2= \begin{cases} 0,&X=0,\\ 1,&X=\pm1. \end{cases}\]Thus, \[P(Y=0)=\frac12, \qquad P(Y=1)=\frac12.\]Hence, \[H(X^2) = -\frac12\log_2\frac12 -\frac12\log_2\frac12 = 1.\]But \[H(X) = -\frac14\log_2\frac14 -\frac12\log_2\frac12 -\frac14\log_2\frac14 = 1.5.\]Therefore, \[H(X)>H(X^2),\]so option (C) is not necessarily true. Option (D): The transformation \[Y=2^X\]is one-to-one. Therefore, \[H(2^X)=H(X).\]Hence, \[H(X)\leq H(2^X)\]is true. \[\boxed{\text{(A), (B) and (D) are correct}}\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume that every function of \(X\) preserves entropy.
  • One-to-one transformations preserve entropy: \[H(g(X))=H(X).\]
  • Many-to-one transformations can reduce entropy.
  • The mapping \[X\mapsto X^2\] is not one-to-one because \[(-x)^2=x^2.\]
  • Maximum entropy for \(K\) outcomes is \[\log_2 K,\]

questions.question: Consider an FM broadcast that employs a pre-emphasis filter with frequency response\[H_{pe}(\omega)=1+j\frac{\omega}{\omega_0}\]where\[\omega_0=10^4 \ \text{rad/s}.\]For the RC network shown below to act as the corresponding de-emphasis filter, the appropriate pair(s) of \((R,C)\) values is/are: [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation: Theory: For perfect compensation,\[H_{de}(\omega)=\frac{1}{H_{pe}(\omega)}.\]The given pre-emphasis filter is \[H_{pe}(\omega)=1+j\frac{\omega}{\omega_0}.\]Hence, \[\left|H_{pe}(\omega)\right|^2 = 1+\left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_0}\right)^2.\]For the RC low-pass network, \[H_{de}(\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega RC}.\]Therefore, \[\left|H_{de}(\omega)\right|^2 = \frac{1}{1+(\omega RC)^2}.\]Since the de-emphasis filter must be the inverse of the pre-emphasis filter, \[\left|H_{pe}(\omega)\right|^2 = \frac{1}{\left|H_{de}(\omega)\right|^2}.\]Substituting the expressions, \[1+\left(\frac{\omega}{\omega_0}\right)^2 = 1+(\omega RC)^2.\]Thus, \[\frac{1}{\omega_0}=RC.\]Given \[\omega_0=10^4 \ \text{rad/s},\] \[RC=\frac{1}{10^4}=10^{-4}\ \text{s}.\]Checking the options: \[(1\,\text{k}\Omega)(0.1\,\mu\text{F}) = 10^3\times 10^{-7} = 10^{-4}\ \text{s}\]which satisfies the condition. \[\boxed{(A) R=1\,\text{k}\Omega,\quad C=0.1\,\mu\text{F}}\]

questions.question: In a circuit, there is a series connection of an ideal resistor and an ideal capacitor. The conduction current (in Amperes) through the resistor is \(2\sin(t + \pi/2)\). The displacement current (in Amperes) through the capacitor is .
questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] For a series connection of an ideal resistor and ideal capacitor, the current through both the elements remains same. Hence, displacement current through the capacitor is equal to the conduction current through the resistor. \[i_{d} = i_{c}\]Given that the conduction current is \(2\sin\left(t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\,\text{A}\), we have: \[\therefore i_{d} = 2\sin\left(t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{2\sin\left(t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\,\text{A}}\]
Key points
  • In a series circuit, the current is identical at all points in the loop.
  • For a capacitor, the conduction current \(i_{c}\) entering the plates is equal to the displacement current \(i_{d}\) between the plates to maintain continuity of current.
  • Displacement current \(i_{d}\) is given by the rate of change of electric flux: \(i_{d} = \epsilon_{0} \dfrac{d\Phi_{E}}{dt}\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume that the displacement current is zero in a series circuit just because there is no physical charge flow between the capacitor plates.
  • Avoid applying phase shifts to the displacement current relative to the conduction current in this context; they are numerically and functionally equal in magnitude and phase for circuit continuity.

questions.question: A waveguide consists of two infinite parallel plates (perfect conductors) at a separation of \(10^{-4}\text{ cm}\), with air as the dielectric. Assume the speed of light in air to be \(3 \times 10^8\text{ m/s}\). The frequency/frequencies of TM waves which can propagate in this waveguide is/are .
questions.explanation:
The Transverse Magnetic (TM) mode with the lowest cut-off frequency is the \(TM_{11}\) mode. The cut-off frequency \(f_{c}\) is given by: \[f_{c}|_{TM_{1}} = \frac{mc}{2a}\] Given \(m = 1\), \(c = 3 \times 10^{10}\,\text{cm/s}\), and waveguide dimension \(a = 10^{-4}\,\text{cm}\): \[f_{c} = \frac{1 \times 3 \times 10^{10}}{2 \times 10^{-4}}\] \[f_{c} = 1.5 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}\] The TM mode that propagate at the lowest cut-off frequency is TM1 mode. Hence \[\boxed{(A,C):6 \times 10^{15}\,\text{Hz},8 \times 10^{14}\,\text{Hz}}\]
Key points
  • The cut-off frequency defines the lower bound for propagation; waves with \(f < f_{c}\) are evanescent.
  • The speed of light \(c\) must be used with the same units as the waveguide dimension \(a\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Confusing TM mode requirements (\(m,n \geq 1\)) with TE mode requirements (\(m\) or \(n\) can be 0) for the rectangular waveguide.

We need to select the contextually appropriate pair of homophones to complete the sentence: ``The is too high for it to be considered .'' Let us analyze the definition and usage of the two words:

questions.question: Some people believe that ``what gets measured, improves''. Some others believe that ``what gets measured, gets gamed''. One possible reason for the difference in the beliefs is the work culture in organizations. In organizations with good work culture, metrics help improve outcomes. However, the same metrics are counterproductive in organizations with poor work culture. Which one of the following is the CORRECT logical inference based on the information in the above passage?
options: Metrics are useful in organizations with poor work culture
Metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture
Metrics are always counterproductive in organizations with good work culture
Metrics are never useful in organizations with good work culture
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the correct logical inference that can be deduced with certainty based *only* on the provided passage text. Let us evaluate the specific conditional assertions given in the passage:
  • The text explicitly states: ``In organizations with good work culture, metrics help improve outcomes.''
  • It also notes that the same metrics are ``counter-productive in organizations with poor work culture.''
Let us evaluate the multiple-choice choices:
  • Choice A directly contradicts the text by claiming metrics are useful in poor cultures.
  • Choice B states: ``Metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture.'' This matches the explicit statement from the text perfectly.
  • Choices C and D introduce absolute qualifiers (``always'', ``never'') that are unsupported by the balanced discussion in the text.
\[\boxed{\text{B. Metrics are useful in organizations with good work culture.}}\]
Key points
  • Valid deductive inferences must rely directly on the explicit conditions stated in the text. Avoid choices that generalize with extreme absolute qualifiers.

questions.question:
The corners and mid-points of the sides of a triangle are named using the distinct letters P, Q, R, S, T and U, but not necessarily in the same order. Consider the following statements:
  • The line joining P and R is parallel to the line joining Q and S.
  • P is placed on the side opposite to the corner T.
  • S and U cannot be placed on the same side.
Which one of the following statements is correct based on the above information?
options: P cannot be placed at a corner
S cannot be placed at a corner
U cannot be placed at a mid-point
R cannot be placed at a corner
questions.explanation:
Given Data: The corners and mid-points of the sides of a triangle are named using the distinct letters \(P, Q, R, S, T\), and \(U\), but not necessarily in the same order.
  • The line joining \(P\) and \(R\) is parallel to the line joining \(Q\) and \(S\).
  • \(P\) is placed on the side opposite corner \(T\).
  • \(S\) and \(U\) cannot be placed on the same side.
Step 1: Position analysis based on given constraints
  • \(P\) is placed on the side opposite to corner \(T\), which means \(P\) lies on the base opposite to vertex \(T\).
  • The line segment \(PR\) is parallel to \(QS\). In a triangle, a line segment joining a mid-point on one side to a mid-point on another side (mid-segment) is always parallel to the base connecting the two corners.
  • Thus, \(PR\) forms a mid-segment parallel to the line segment \(QS\).
Step 2: Determining the nature of point \(S\)
  • Since \(PR\) is parallel to \(QS\), \(S\) must be placed at a mid-point along one of the sides of the inner mid-segment structure rather than a corner.
  • Therefore, \(S\) cannot be placed at a corner.
This corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. S cannot be placed at a corner}}\]
Key points
  • Midpoint Parallel Theorem: The line segment connecting the midpoints of two sides of a triangle is parallel to the opposite base side connecting the two corners. This structural rule automatically fixes the topological positions of parallel point pairs.

  • Heel (noun) refers to the back part of the human foot below the ankle.
  • Heal (verb) means to become sound or healthy again, or to mend after an injury.
Substituting these definitions into the sentence structure yields a contextually logical statement: ``An injury to your foot anatomy (heel) may take longer to mend and recover (heal).'' Thus, the correct sequence is heel / heal, which corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. heel / heal}}\]
Key points
  • Identifying homophones relies on distinguishing between noun anatomical descriptors (heel) and active verbs of cellular biological recovery (heal).
